title: The board underneath
intro: The motherboard is mostly wiring, and the interesting history is in what those wires connect to. Slots appear when a job is too big for the main processor and disappear once it absorbs the job back, so reading an old board tells you exactly what the machine of that year could not do on its own. It is also where the PC's least glamorous failures happen: bent pins, dead batteries, bulging capacitors and settings that fight each other.

blocks.title: One shared bus, and setting everything by hand
blocks.text: A bus is a set of wires every expansion card listens to. In the original design all cards shared one path running at the speed of the slowest device on it, which was fine when a card was a serial port and impossible once cards were pushing video. Worse, nothing configured itself. Each card needed to be told which interrupt line and which block of memory to use, and you told it by moving small plastic jumpers or flicking switches on the card itself.

blocks.name: ISA, 8-bit
blocks.spec: 8 data lines, 4.77 MHz, ~2.4 MB/s, 5 slots
blocks.text: IBM published the full technical reference, including the circuit diagrams and a printed listing of the BIOS code, so anyone could build a card that worked. That decision created the entire PC industry within five years. It also meant IBM could not stop anyone from building the whole machine, and the standard stopped belonging to IBM at all.

blocks.name: Interrupts, DMA channels and jumpers
blocks.spec: 8 interrupt lines on the PC, 15 usable on the AT
blocks.text: An interrupt line is how a card gets the processor's attention, and there were very few of them. Every card had to be set to a line no other card was using, along with a memory address and often a DMA channel, and you set these by physically moving jumpers according to a table in the manual. Get it wrong and the machine would hang, or the sound card would work until you moved the mouse. Installing hardware meant keeping a written list of what was using what. This is worth describing to students in detail, because it is the problem the next fifteen years of standards exist to solve.

blocks.name: ISA, 16-bit
blocks.spec: 16 data lines, 8 MHz, ~8 MB/s
blocks.text: A second connector added in line behind the first, so old 8-bit cards still fitted in the front section and ignored the rest. Backward compatibility by physically extending the slot, which is a very PC solution and one you can still see in the shape of a modern PCI Express connector.

blocks.name: The AT power connector
blocks.spec: Two 6-pin plugs, not keyed against each other
blocks.text: The power supply connected through two separate plugs that fitted the socket in either order, and only one order was correct. The rule people memorised was to keep the black wires together in the middle. Getting it wrong destroyed the board. ATX later fixed this by making the connector a single shape that only fits one way, which is the sort of design change that never gets celebrated and prevents thousands of expensive mistakes.

blocks.name: IBM Micro Channel
blocks.spec: 32-bit, 40 MB/s, licence and royalties required
blocks.text: A genuinely better bus, faster and self-configuring years before anyone else managed it, and IBM's attempt to take the standard back. Manufacturers who wanted to use it had to pay royalties, and IBM also wanted back payments on the clones they had already sold. The industry refused, nine companies formed a group to build their own answer, and Micro Channel ended up a minority option on IBM's own machines. Technical superiority loses to licensing terms often enough on this site that it is worth treating as a rule rather than an exception.

blocks.name: EISA
blocks.spec: 32-bit, 33 MB/s, accepts existing ISA cards
blocks.text: The rival group's answer, built by extending the ISA slot downwards with a second row of contacts so an old card sat shallowly and a new one seated fully. As fast as Micro Channel, no licence, and compatible with everything people already owned. It was expensive to implement and stayed mostly in servers, but it made the point, and Micro Channel never recovered.

blocks.title: PCI, ATX, and the shape of the modern machine
blocks.text: Three things settled in this stretch that are still true of the board in this case. A bus that configured its own cards, a physical layout that has barely changed in thirty years, and a single connector intended to replace all the others on the back panel. This is also where the board split into two support chips, which is worth understanding because both have since been eaten.

blocks.name: VESA Local Bus
blocks.spec: 32-bit, 33 MHz, ~132 MB/s, usually 2 slots
blocks.text: A slot wired almost directly onto the 486 processor's own bus, which made it very fast and extremely fussy. The cards were long and heavy, the electrical loading meant most boards could only run two or three slots and often only at reduced speed, and the whole design was tied to one processor generation. When the Pentium arrived it died within about two years. A useful example of a shortcut that works brilliantly and cannot be carried forward.

blocks.name: PCI
blocks.spec: 32-bit, 33 MHz, 133 MB/s, processor independent
blocks.text: Fast, not tied to any one processor, and cards could be asked what they were and told what resources to use, in software, at startup. That last part ended the jumper era. Intel developed it and then handed it to an industry group rather than charging for it, having watched what happened to Micro Channel. PCI outlasted every bus that came before it and stayed on consumer boards for twenty-four years.

blocks.name: Plug and Play
blocks.spec: Automatic resource assignment, arrived with Windows 95
blocks.text: The operating system, the BIOS and the card negotiating who gets which interrupt, with no jumpers and no written list. When it worked it was transformative. When it did not, which was often in the first few years because ISA cards in the same machine could not participate, it was nicknamed Plug and Pray. Worth knowing that a technology can be both a genuine breakthrough and a running joke at the same time.

blocks.name: ATX form factor
blocks.spec: 305 x 244 mm, rear I/O panel, keyed 20-pin power, software power off
blocks.text: Thirty years on, the board in this machine follows the same standard, which is why a case bought today fits a board designed to a specification older than most of the people reading this. Intel published it and did not charge for it. It moved all the connectors to one rear panel instead of a tangle of ribbon cables to slot covers, placed the processor where the power supply fan would draw air over it, and let the operating system switch the machine off, which the older AT design physically could not do because the power switch was a mains switch wired to the front of the case.

blocks.name: USB 1.0
blocks.spec: 12 Mb/s, powered, hot pluggable, up to 127 devices
blocks.text: Before this, a mouse, keyboard, printer, modem, scanner and joystick each used a different connector, and adding a device often meant opening the case and choosing an interrupt. USB replaced all of it with one plug that supplies power, works while the machine is running, and needs no configuration. Nobody used it for two years because there were no devices, and there were no devices because nobody used it. The 1998 iMac, which shipped with USB and nothing else, is usually credited with breaking that deadlock on the PC side as well.

blocks.name: AGP
blocks.spec: 1x at 266 MB/s, rising to 8x at 2.1 GB/s by 2002
blocks.text: A slot for one card only, wired straight to the memory controller, because graphics had become the one device capable of saturating PCI by itself. It also let the card use main system memory for textures when its own ran out, which sounded better than it worked in practice.

blocks.name: AGP voltage keying
blocks.spec: 3.3 V for 1x and 2x, 1.5 V for 4x and 8x
blocks.text: As AGP got faster it dropped to a lower voltage, and the slot gained a notch in a different place so an incompatible card would not fit. Some boards had a universal slot with no notch at all, and forcing the wrong card into the wrong board could damage both. A good illustration of physical keying as a safety feature, and of what happens when a standard adds variants faster than buyers can keep track of them.

blocks.name: Northbridge and southbridge
blocks.spec: Two chips: fast memory and graphics, slow everything else
blocks.text: The board's support logic split in two. The northbridge sat close to the processor handling memory and the graphics slot, and needed a heatsink. The southbridge handled drives, USB, audio and the slow buses, and did not. Together they were called the chipset, and for about ten years which chipset a board used mattered more than the brand on the box, because it determined what memory you could fit, how fast the bus ran and whether the machine was stable at all. Both have since been absorbed, the northbridge into the processor and the southbridge into a single remaining chip.

blocks.title: The capacitor plague, and other things that went quietly wrong
blocks.text: This stretch produced the largest hardware quality failure in PC history, affecting millions of boards from nearly every manufacturer, and it is barely known outside enthusiast circles. It is also the period when a chipset could be recalled, and when picking the wrong one meant living with instability you could not fix.

blocks.name: The capacitor plague begins
blocks.spec: Electrolytic capacitors bulging, venting and leaking after 1 to 3 years
blocks.text: Boards began failing in a distinctive way: the small cylindrical capacitors near the processor swelled, their tops split along a scored cross, and a crust leaked out. Machines would fail to start, restart at random, or become unstable under load. The usual account is that an electrolyte formula was copied incompletely by a competitor, so capacitors made with it corroded from the inside and generated hydrogen until they burst. The faulty parts spread through the supply chain into boards from most major manufacturers between roughly 1999 and 2007. Dell alone set aside around $300 million over affected office machines, and the motherboard maker Abit, one of the best regarded enthusiast brands of the era, never recovered and left the business. It is the clearest case on this site of a failure that has nothing to do with design or specifications and everything to do with a component two suppliers down the chain, and the visible symptom makes it easy to show students a photograph and have them recognise it.

blocks.name: The Intel 820 recall
blocks.spec: Around a million boards recalled over a memory translator chip
blocks.text: Intel's 820 chipset was built for the expensive RDRAM memory nobody wanted to buy, so Intel added a translator chip to let ordinary SDRAM be used instead. The translator turned out to cause data corruption and system crashes, and Intel recalled roughly a million boards. It is a useful reminder that a bolted-on compatibility layer is a design risk, and it belongs beside the RDRAM entry on the memory page as part of the same expensive misjudgement.

blocks.name: USB 2.0
blocks.spec: 480 Mb/s
blocks.text: Forty times faster, which is what made external hard drives and memory sticks practical and finished off the floppy disk. It is also where the confusing habit of reusing the USB name for very different speeds begins, and that habit has since become considerably worse.

blocks.name: Chipsets and the stability lottery
blocks.spec: Intel, VIA, SiS, ALi, nForce
blocks.text: For several years, buying a board meant researching its chipset rather than its brand. Some third party chipsets were noticeably cheaper and had well documented problems with particular sound cards, hard drive controllers or graphics cards, requiring driver packages installed in a specific order. Machines that crashed for no visible reason were often a chipset and driver mismatch rather than anything the owner had done. Integration has quietly removed most of this, which is progress that is hard to see because it consists of an entire category of problem no longer existing.

blocks.name: Serial ATA
blocks.spec: 150 MB/s, 7-wire cable
blocks.text: The wide ribbon cable that had run from the board to the drives since 1986 finally went, taking with it the need to set each drive as master or slave with a jumper on the back.

blocks.name: BTX, the form factor that did not happen
blocks.spec: Intel's ATX replacement, abandoned by 2007
blocks.text: Designed around the problem of the moment, which was that the Pentium 4 produced more heat than a case could reasonably remove. BTX reorganised the board so cool air from the front passed over the processor first and everything sat in one straight airflow path. It was a sound piece of engineering aimed at a problem that then disappeared, because the Core 2 arrived using half the power and ATX cases were suddenly adequate again. Intel abandoned it. Solving today's problem with a standard that takes five years to adopt is a real risk, and this is the cleanest example of it.

blocks.name: LGA 775, and the pins move
blocks.spec: 775 contacts on the socket instead of pins on the chip
blocks.text: Processors used to have pins sticking out of them, and bending one meant a ruined processor. Intel inverted it: the socket holds hundreds of delicate sprung pins and the chip has flat gold pads. Higher pin counts became possible, and the fragile part moved from the item you bought to the item already in your machine. It also moved the blame, since a bent socket pin is usually not covered by a board warranty. AMD kept pins on the chip until 2022, so for eighteen years the answer to whether a bent pin was your problem or the manufacturer's depended on which brand you had bought.

blocks.name: PCI Express 1.0
blocks.spec: 250 MB/s per lane, x1 to x16 slots
blocks.text: Not a shared bus at all. Every device gets its own dedicated pair of wires in each direction, called a lane, and takes as many lanes as it needs. Nothing waits for anything else. A x16 graphics slot and a x1 capture card use the same standard and differ only in how many lanes are wired to them, and a short card will happily run in a long slot. This removed the last reason for having separate buses for different jobs, and everything on a modern board is now some number of PCIe lanes.

blocks.name: The memory controller leaves the board
blocks.spec: AMD from 2003, Intel from 2008
blocks.text: The northbridge's main job moved into the processor, removing a whole chip from the path between the processor and its memory. One consequence catches people out: the memory types and speeds a board supports are now decided by the processor you fit, not by the board, which is why a board's specification sheet lists different memory support for different chip generations.

blocks.name: PCIe 2.0
blocks.spec: 500 MB/s per lane, 8 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: Each generation of PCI Express has roughly doubled the rate per lane while keeping the same physical slot, so a new card fits an old board and simply runs slower. Nineteen years of that is a remarkable run for a connector, and it is why a graphics card from 2025 will physically fit a board from 2004.

blocks.title: Everything moves onto the processor, and the board becomes power delivery
blocks.text: One by one the board's functions were absorbed. What is left is the wiring, the sockets, the firmware and, increasingly, the electrical engineering needed to feed a processor that can ask for three hundred watts in a few millionths of a second. The most meaningful difference between a cheap board and an expensive one is now something with no marketing name that most buyers never look at.

blocks.name: USB 3.0, and the naming problem
blocks.spec: 5 Gb/s, later renamed three times
blocks.text: Ten times USB 2.0, which made external SSDs sensible. It was then renamed USB 3.1 Gen 1, then USB 3.2 Gen 1, then marketed as USB 5Gbps, all describing the identical thing, while faster versions reused the same names with different numbers after them. The standards body has made the speed of a USB port genuinely difficult to determine from its name, which is worth pointing at whenever someone assumes standards bodies always reduce confusion.

blocks.name: PCIe 3.0
blocks.spec: ~1 GB/s per lane, 16 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: Current for eight years, and still enough for most graphics cards well after it was superseded. A card asking for more lanes than the board has spare simply runs at fewer, usually with a smaller loss than people expect.

blocks.name: UEFI replaces the BIOS
blocks.spec: Graphical setup, GPT partitions, drives over 2.2 TB, fast startup
blocks.text: The BIOS dated to 1981, still started the machine in a mode designed for the 8088, and could not boot from a drive larger than 2.2 terabytes. UEFI is closer to a small operating system that runs before the real one: it understands file systems, has drivers, supports a mouse, and can run programs of its own. That is more capable and also a larger surface for things to go wrong on, since firmware now contains enough code to have security flaws of its own.

blocks.name: Secure Boot
blocks.spec: Firmware refuses to run unsigned boot code
blocks.text: The machine checks a cryptographic signature before running anything at startup, which genuinely blocks a class of malware that loads before the operating system can defend itself. It also meant the keys deciding what a computer is allowed to boot were held by Microsoft, and Linux users argued forcefully about whether a machine you own should refuse to run software you chose. The compromise was a small signed program that hands over to anything else, and the ability to turn the feature off. A good discussion topic, because both positions are reasonable.

blocks.name: M.2, and the lanes it takes with it
blocks.spec: PCIe x4 or SATA, 22 x 80 mm, no cable
blocks.text: A slot flat on the board holding a drive with no cable and no power lead, which is where the storage in this machine lives. The catch appears in the manual rather than on the box: a processor provides a fixed number of PCIe lanes, so filling the second M.2 slot commonly disables two SATA ports or drops the graphics slot from sixteen lanes to eight. Nothing warns you at the time. It is the modern equivalent of the interrupt conflict, solved in software instead of jumpers but still a fixed resource being shared.

blocks.name: Socket AM4 and the BIOS chip argument
blocks.spec: One socket, 2016 to 2024, five processor generations
blocks.text: AMD kept one socket alive for eight years, so a board bought in 2017 could take a processor released in 2022, which is unheard of. It nearly came apart over something mundane: the chip storing the firmware was only 16 megabytes, and supporting every processor generation would not fit. AMD announced that older boards would not get support for the newest chips, customers who had bought partly on the promise of a long-lived socket reacted angrily, and AMD reversed the decision within weeks by letting manufacturers ship firmware that dropped support for older processors instead. A storage limit in a component nobody thinks about turned into a public argument about what a promise is worth.

blocks.name: The last ISA-descended slot goes
blocks.spec: Conventional PCI removed from mainstream chipsets
blocks.text: PCI slots quietly stopped appearing on consumer boards, twenty-four years after the standard arrived and thirty-six after the ISA slot it replaced. Industrial and laboratory equipment kept them alive far longer, because a working machine controlling a scientific instrument is not replaced just because its bus is unfashionable.

blocks.name: Voltage regulator modules
blocks.spec: The circuitry converting 12 V to the ~1.2 V a processor uses
blocks.text: The single biggest difference between a cheap board and an expensive one, and the one nobody advertises clearly. A processor runs at around 1.2 volts and can draw over 200 amps, changing demand in millionths of a second. The regulator does that conversion, and it is built as several parallel stages called phases, with heatsinks over them. A weak regulator on a budget board will get hot and quietly reduce the processor's speed to protect itself, so the same processor is measurably slower in one board than another with no setting to explain it. If a student takes one buying lesson from this page, it is that the specification that matters most here is the one printed smallest.

blocks.name: PCIe 4.0
blocks.spec: ~2 GB/s per lane
blocks.text: Fast enough that board makers had to start using better circuit board materials and adding signal repeater chips, because copper traces were losing too much of the signal over the distance from the socket to the far end of the board. This is why boards got more expensive at this generation for no feature you can see.

blocks.name: Thunderbolt and USB4
blocks.spec: 40 Gb/s, PCIe lanes over a cable
blocks.text: Thunderbolt carries PCI Express itself over a cable, which means an external box can hold a graphics card and appear to the machine as though it were plugged into a slot. Intel donated the specification and it became the basis of USB4, so the same connector now carries power, video, data and expansion slots. It is the endpoint of the process that started when USB replaced six different plugs in 1996.

blocks.name: PCIe 5.0
blocks.spec: ~4 GB/s per lane, 64 GB/s at x16
blocks.text: The current standard on this board, and the reason it can run a graphics card and two fast drives without any of them slowing the others. Signal integrity is now hard enough that the number of usable slots is limited by physics rather than by space on the board.

blocks.name: The CMOS battery is still there
blocks.spec: CR2032 coin cell, about 3 volts, lasts 5 to 10 years
blocks.text: One component has survived unchanged since the 1980s. A coin cell keeps the real time clock running while the machine is unplugged. When it dies the machine forgets the date, complains at startup and sometimes loses its settings, and the fix costs about a pound. Worth pointing out to students because it is the one repair on this entire board that anyone can do, and because a computer that has forgotten what year it is will also fail to connect to secure websites, which makes a dead battery look like a much more alarming fault than it is.

blocks.name: What is left on the board
blocks.spec: One socket, four memory slots, two PCIe slots, two M.2 slots
blocks.text: Compare that to a 1996 board with six or seven slots, nearly all of them occupied. Sound, networking, wireless, USB, storage control, graphics output and the memory controller have all been absorbed into the processor or the one remaining chipset chip. The board is now wiring, sockets, firmware and power delivery. The empty slot in this machine is the honest summary of forty years of progress: the jobs did not disappear, the cards did.

blocks.title: What to take from this
blocks.text: Two patterns run through the whole page. Standards win on licensing terms and compatibility rather than on merit, which is Micro Channel against EISA, PCI succeeding because Intel gave it away, and ATX outliving the better-engineered BTX. And the board's history is one long process of absorption, where every function that once justified a slot ends up inside something else. When you next open an old machine, count the cards and work out what each one was for, because each is a job that computer could not do by itself.

blocks.label: The cards those slots held
blocks.text: Every slot on an old board had something in it. What those cards did, and what swallowed each of them, is the other half of this story.
